title: Through the Hourglass
caption: The hourglass-shaped remnant CK Vulpeculae, imaged by ALMA
celestial: CK Vulpeculae · constellation Vulpecula · about 2000 light-years away (source figure)

recognition.text: ESO Picture of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: This image from the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA) gives the best view to date of the central part of CK Vulpeculae, an hourglass-shaped remnant. It traces dust and emission in and around the object and reveals its intricate structure. At its heart is a warped, dusty disc, along with gaseous jets that suggest a central system is pushing material outward.

CK Vulpeculae may be the oldest object of its kind ever cataloged. It was first thought to be a nova, but pinning down what it is has proved hard, and several explanations have been tried and dropped. The current view is that it formed when two stars collided, though astronomers still debate what kind of stars they were.

Most novae are explained by runaway explosions between two close stars in a binary system, and CK Vulpeculae never fitted that picture well. These ALMA observations are the first to bring the system into focus and may help settle a 348-year-old mystery.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (0.33 x 0.18 arcminutes) and distance (2000 light years), the frame spans roughly 0.2 × 0.1 light-years. Its light set out about 2,000 years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: Made with ALMA in its Band 6, which observes millimeter-wavelength light. The color mapping isn't published.
filters: 1.324534 mm · Millimeter Continuum (Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array Band 6)
understand.eye: Millimeter-wavelength light is invisible to the eye, so the colors are a translation of signals from dust and gas that no one could see directly.

explore: French monk and astronomer Père Dom Anthelme first spotted the outburst on 20 June 1670, when it was easy to see with the naked eye. Over the next two years it brightened and faded, disappeared and reappeared twice, and then vanished for good. The object lies about 2000 light-years away in the constellation of Vulpecula.
alt: An hourglass-shaped structure mapped in millimeter-wavelength light, with a warped, dusty disc at its center.
